distractors.c: Rewriting history removes the commit from this repository only; forks, clones and caches keep it, and the key itself stays valid.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat an exposed credential as compromised and rotate it, rather than trying to un-publish it.

references.title: GitHub Docs: Push protection
MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001 Credentials In Files

questions.subtopic: personal instance of a sanctioned cloud service
questions.question: A bank uses a cloud office suite and its web gateway allows the suite's domains. An investigation shows that an employee signed in from a bank laptop to a personal account on the same suite and uploaded internal files to it. Which control closes this specific gap without disrupting use of the bank's own tenant?

options.text: Block the suite's domains at the gateway and re-allow them only for a list of named business users
Restrict sign-ins from bank devices and networks so that only the bank's own tenant can be used
Add an inline content rule that blocks any upload of confidential files to the suite's domains
Move the suite to the unsanctioned category so that the shadow IT report flags every upload to it

explanation.correct: The bank's tenant and the personal account share the same domains, so any control that works on domains or URL categories treats them alike. The fix must recognise the account or tenant: tenant restrictions, such as Microsoft Entra tenant restrictions v2, limit which external tenants and accounts users can reach from the organisation's networks and devices, so a personal account simply cannot sign in. CASB and SSE products achieve the same with instance-aware rules that tell the corporate instance from personal ones. ATT&CK tracks the behaviour as T1567.002, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage. The investigation itself continues separately: what was uploaded, and whether the files can be recovered or deleted.

distractors.a: Named users can still sign in to personal accounts once the domains are allowed for them, and everyone else loses a service the bank depends on.
distractors.c: The rule cannot tell the two instances apart, so it also blocks staff legitimately saving confidential files to the bank's own tenant.
distractors.d: The sanctioned suite is the bank's main platform; marking it unsanctioned floods the report with legitimate use and still does not separate the instances.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you spot that personal and corporate instances of one service look identical to domain-based controls.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Configure tenant restrictions v2
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: Gateway logs show that 40 employees across several departments uploaded PDF files to a free online file-conversion website that IT has never assessed. No DLP rule matched. How should the L1 analyst classify and route this?

options.text: As shadow IT: log it, route it to cloud-app review and check whether uploads held sensitive data
As command-and-control traffic from malware, so all 40 laptops should be isolated straight away
As a disciplinary case, reporting all 40 employees to HR for breaching the acceptable-use policy
As benign, because no DLP rule matched, which shows the files cannot have contained any company data

explanation.correct: Shadow IT is any service used for work without IT's assessment or approval. The risk is that company files are processed and stored by a third party nobody has vetted, with unknown retention and terms. The pattern here (many users, many departments, one convenient tool) is a business need without an approved option, not an attack. The right route is the organisation's cloud-app governance: assess the service, then sanction it, offer an approved alternative or block it, and tell users why. Discovery tools support this by matching gateway and firewall logs against an app catalogue; Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, for example, scores discovered apps on more than 90 risk factors. A 'no match' is not proof of clean content, since a scanned PDF without OCR, for one, would not match, so sample what was uploaded.

distractors.b: Dozens of users choosing the same well-known site through a browser points to a convenient tool, not malware beaconing; isolating 40 laptops would be over-containment.
distractors.c: Without an approved alternative or clear communication, mass disciplinary action punishes a process gap; individual cases go to HR only if the data involved warrants it.
distractors.d: A DLP rule that did not match may simply not have been able to read the files, for example scanned PDFs without OCR.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat shadow IT as a governance and data-exposure question rather than a malware or HR problem.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Discover and manage Shadow IT
Microsoft Learn: Cloud app discovery overview

questions.question: A company's managed laptops are covered by endpoint DLP for USB and web uploads, a web gateway and email DLP. An insider-risk review finds that the laptops' built-in peer-to-peer wireless sharing feature can send files straight to a nearby phone. Which TWO controls address this channel? (Choose two.)

options.text: A web gateway DLP rule that inspects every upload to file-sharing and personal cloud storage websites
A device-management restriction that disables or limits the peer-to-peer sharing feature
An email DLP rule that blocks attachments with sensitive content sent to personal addresses
Network flow alerts on unusually large outbound transfers from managed laptops to the internet
An endpoint DLP rule restricting file copies to unapproved Bluetooth or wireless-sharing apps

explanation.correct: Peer-to-peer sharing such as AirDrop finds the other device over Bluetooth and moves the file over a direct device-to-device wireless link, so the transfer never touches the corporate network, the gateway or the mail system. ATT&CK groups this under T1011, Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium (T1011.001 for Bluetooth). Only controls on the device itself can see or stop it: a device-management restriction that turns the feature off or limits it on managed laptops, and an endpoint DLP rule on the copy action. Microsoft Purview Endpoint DLP, for example, has a 'Copy or move using unallowed Bluetooth app' activity driven by a list of unallowed Bluetooth apps in its endpoint settings. Endpoint telemetry (EDR, OS logs) then provides the evidence for investigations.

distractors.a: The gateway only sees traffic that goes through it; a direct device-to-device link never does.
distractors.c: Email DLP covers the mail channel; this transfer involves no message at all.
distractors.d: The data does not go to the internet, so there is no outbound flow from the laptop to alert on.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you map each exfiltration channel to the sensor that can actually see it, especially channels that bypass the network.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1011.001 Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
Microsoft Learn: Learn about Endpoint data loss prevention

questions.question: A bank client asks its MSSP why no DLP alert fired when an employee shared his screen, showing a customer list, with an external party during a video call. The bank runs endpoint, email and collaboration DLP with OCR enabled. What should the MSSP analyst explain?

options.text: OCR should have read the shared screen, so the OCR setup is faulty and needs to be raised with the DLP vendor
The external party must have joined anonymously, and anonymous participants are excluded from all DLP scanning
DLP inspects files and messages, not a live video stream; the evidence is the meeting and application logs
The customer list was below the rule's instance threshold, so the threshold has to be lowered for meetings

explanation.correct: DLP engines, OCR included, inspect content objects: files, messages, attachments and images in motion or at rest. A live screen share is a stream of video frames shown to the other side; no file or message is created for DLP to evaluate. The investigation therefore uses other records: the meeting's participant and presenter details (who was external, who shared, for how long) and the CRM's access log for the list that was displayed. Controls belong to the meeting platform and to process: restrict screen sharing and recording for external participants, hold client-data discussions only in meetings the bank organises, and train staff. If the meeting was recorded, the recording is a file and follows the organiser's storage and permissions; in Teams, for example, it is uploaded to the organiser's OneDrive or to SharePoint for channel meetings, and external attendees see it only if it is explicitly shared with them.

distractors.a: OCR works on images and files the DLP engine receives; it does not watch a live stream, so there is nothing faulty to report.
distractors.b: Who the participant was does not matter here: no participant type makes a live screen share inspectable by content DLP.
distractors.d: No content reached the rule, so there was no instance count to compare with a threshold.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can explain a DLP blind spot to a client honestly and point to the evidence and controls that do apply.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Manage Teams recording policies for meetings and events
Microsoft Learn: Learn about data loss prevention

questions.question: A bank inspects web uploads at an on-premises proxy. Remote staff use a VPN with split tunnelling, which sends only internal-application traffic through the tunnel. Bank files are found on a home-working employee's personal cloud storage account, but the proxy has no record of any upload. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The employee must have used an anonymising proxy, which hides traffic from every control the bank operates
The proxy discarded the log entries because the uploads were encrypted with TLS
Uploads to personal cloud storage use a special protocol that web proxies are unable to log
Internet traffic went straight out of the home connection and never passed the proxy

explanation.correct: With split tunnelling, only traffic for internal destinations goes through the VPN; everything bound for the internet, a personal cloud account included, leaves through the home router. An on-premises proxy cannot inspect or log what never reaches it. Evidence for the investigation has to come from the laptop: endpoint DLP events for uploads to cloud service domains, EDR process and network telemetry, browser history. The lasting fixes are controls that travel with the device: endpoint DLP, which enforces on the laptop whatever network it is on, and a cloud-delivered gateway client that steers web traffic to inspection from anywhere, or a forced tunnel for internet traffic. ATT&CK tracks the behaviour as T1567.002, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage.

distractors.a: No extra tool is needed to explain the gap: the VPN design already sends this traffic around the proxy, and endpoint controls would still see an anonymiser on the laptop.
distractors.b: A proxy logs TLS connections even when it cannot read their content; encryption hides the payload, not the fact of the connection.
distractors.c: Web-based cloud storage uploads are ordinary HTTPS requests, which proxies log routinely when the traffic passes through them.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check the network path a remote user's traffic actually takes before trusting a perimeter control's silence.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Learn about Endpoint data loss prevention
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: A remote employee's managed laptop was offline for three days while she travelled. Because the DLP console shows no endpoint events from that laptop for those three days, the endpoint DLP policies on it cannot have been enforced during that time.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: Enforcement and reporting are separate. Microsoft documents for Purview Endpoint DLP that when a Windows device is offline, the policies already pushed to it keep being enforced on existing files, but the enforcement events only appear in Activity explorer after the device is back online. Policy changes made while it was offline do not reach it until it reconnects, and the Devices list shows it as out of sync. For an analyst, an empty timeline from a device that has been offline means 'not uploaded yet', not 'no activity' and not 'no protection': check the device's last-seen and sync status, and look again once it reconnects.

distractors.a: This mixes up enforcement, which happens on the laptop, with reporting, which needs a connection. The policies kept running offline; only the events were held back.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand where the agent enforces and where the console learns about it, so that you do not misread a gap in telemetry.

questions.subtopic: what EDR, SIEM, SOAR and identity add to DLP
questions.question: A DLP alert says a user uploaded a customer file to a personal storage site. Match each integrated source to the signal it adds to the investigation.

right.text: Resignation or contract end date, which places the activity inside a departure window
Which process created, compressed or uploaded the file, and what launched that process
The exact content matches and the rule that fired
The same enrichment and response steps run automatically every time, such as opening the case and pulling user context
MFA result, location, device compliance and sign-in risk for the session that did the upload
Months of correlated history from other sources, such as earlier proxy, VPN and badge events

explanation.correct: Each source answers a different question about the same alert. EDR tells how the file left (process lineage: an archiver run before a browser upload looks very different from a sync client). The identity provider tells who was really behind the session (MFA, unusual location, unmanaged device, risk detections), which separates a compromised account from an insider. The SIEM keeps and correlates logs from many sources over time, so it shows whether this is the first upload or the tenth. SOAR produces no new telemetry: it orchestrates the enrichment and response steps consistently and quickly. The HR system supplies context such as a resignation date, which is why insider-risk tools import it. The content match and the rule (r3) come from the DLP alert itself.

distractors.l3: A SIEM may display the DLP alert, but the content match (r3) is produced by DLP; the SIEM's own value is correlation across retained sources.
distractors.l4: SOAR does not collect telemetry of its own, so it cannot be the source of sign-in or process details; it pulls them from the other tools.
distractors.l1: EDR sees processes and files on the endpoint, not the sign-in risk of the session (r5), which comes from the identity provider.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know what each tool in a SOC stack contributes, rather than treating them as interchangeable consoles.

questions.question: An MSSP builds a SOAR playbook for a bank client's high-severity DLP alerts about customer data sent to personal email addresses. Put the playbook stages in order.

options.text: Enrich automatically: department, manager, HR status, recent sign-in risk and the user's DLP history
After analyst approval, run the containment action agreed in the client's runbook and notify the client contact
Ingest the alert and de-duplicate it against cases already open for the same user and file
Record the verdict and every action with timestamps, and feed the verdict into rule-tuning metrics
Present the enriched case to an analyst, who decides whether it is a true positive

explanation.correct: De-duplicate first, so that one user sending ten emails produces one case and enrichment is not run ten times. Enrichment comes next because it is cheap, automatic and is exactly what the analyst needs to decide quickly. The decision stays with a human: containment that touches a bank employee's mailbox has business and HR consequences, so the playbook waits for an analyst's true-positive verdict (human in the loop) instead of acting on the raw alert. Only then does it run the containment the client's runbook allows and notify the client contact as the contract requires. Finally, recording verdicts and timestamps gives the audit trail and the data (false-positive rate per rule, time to contain) that tuning and service reporting depend on.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you automate the repetitive parts and keep a human decision before actions that affect people.

questions.question: An MSSP advises a bank client on offboarding an external contractor whose engagement ends on Friday. Put the steps in order.

options.text: At the end time, disable the account, revoke active sessions and rotate any shared secrets the contractor knew
Review the contractor's recent data activity (downloads, external sharing, DLP alerts) before departure
A few days later, run an access review to confirm no accounts, keys or group memberships remain
Confirm the end date with the contract owner and set the account to expire at that time
Transfer ownership of the contractor's files and remove the external shares they created

explanation.correct: Everything hangs on a confirmed end date, so start there and make the account expire automatically even if someone forgets. Review recent activity while the contractor is still working, because a departure window is when bulk downloads and sharing to personal accounts tend to happen, and a finding then can still be handled calmly with the contract owner. Transfer file ownership and remove shares before the account is disabled, while the owner can still be acted on cleanly. At the end time, disabling sign-in is not enough on its own: Microsoft Entra guidance, for example, pairs disabling the account with revoking sessions, because tokens already issued stay valid until they expire. Shared secrets the contractor knew must be rotated. Finally, an access review catches what the main account did not cover, such as local accounts, API keys or group memberships in other systems.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat offboarding as a data-protection process with a pre-departure review, not just an account switch-off.

questions.question: A company in the EU is launching an insider-risk programme that scores employees' file, email and web activity. Which TWO design choices best support the programme's legal and ethical defensibility? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run a data protection impact assessment and document why each indicator is necessary and proportionate
Keep the programme secret from employees, so that potential insiders cannot adapt their behaviour to avoid detection
Show analysts pseudonymised identities by default, revealing names only when a case is escalated
Collect every available activity signal for all employees and keep it indefinitely in case an investigation needs it later
Let line managers browse the risk scores of their own team members so that they can spot problems early and intervene

explanation.correct: Systematic monitoring of employees is high-risk processing, so a data protection impact assessment (GDPR art. 35) before go-live is the expected starting point, together with a documented necessity and proportionality case for each indicator. Pseudonymisation applies data minimisation (art. 5(1)(c)) to the analysts themselves: they triage behaviour, not people, and names are revealed only when a case meets the escalation threshold. Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management, for example, has a privacy setting to show anonymised versions of usernames in alerts and cases. Both choices also help with works councils and employee trust, which a programme needs in order to last.

distractors.b: Transparency is a GDPR principle (art. 5(1)(a)) and employees must be informed about processing of their data (art. 13); covert monitoring is at most an exception for a specific investigation, not a programme design.
distractors.d: Collecting everything and keeping it forever breaches data minimisation and storage limitation (art. 5(1)(c) and (e)) and adds exposure without improving detection.
distractors.e: Risk scores are sensitive and often wrong at the individual level; giving them to line managers invites misuse and bias. Access belongs to a small, trained team on a need-to-know basis.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can build an insider-risk programme that a works council, a privacy regulator and employees would accept.

questions.question: An MSSP prepares a quarterly DLP effectiveness report for a bank client's risk committee. Which measure gives the committee the most meaningful evidence that the controls actually reduce leakage risk?

options.text: The total number of DLP alerts raised this quarter compared with last quarter, where a fall is read as users leaking less data
Coverage per channel, proven by regular test transfers of synthetic data, plus each rule's true-positive rate
The number of DLP rules deployed, broken down by channel, to show how far the programme has been extended this quarter
The share of employees who completed the annual data-protection training, compared with the target set by the committee

explanation.correct: A risk committee needs evidence that controls work, not that they are busy. Coverage proven by testing answers 'would we catch it?': seeded transfers of synthetic sensitive data through each channel (email, web upload, USB, cloud sharing, AI apps) on a schedule show which channels detect or block and which have silently stopped, for example because agents are unhealthy. Each rule's true-positive rate answers 'can we trust the alerts?', since a rule that is 95% noise hides real incidents. Together with time to triage and contain confirmed incidents, these are outcome measures. The others are inputs or activity: alert counts fall when agents break as well as when behaviour improves, rule counts measure effort, and training completion measures attendance, not behaviour.

distractors.a: Alert volume is ambiguous: it drops after tuning, after an outage or when agents stop reporting, so a fall proves nothing about leakage.
distractors.c: More rules is effort, not effect; badly tuned rules can even make detection worse by burying real alerts.
distractors.d: Training completion is a useful input metric, but it shows attendance, not whether data still leaks or whether controls catch it.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can report DLP in terms of tested outcomes that a non-technical committee can rely on.

questions.question: A bank's insider-risk tool starts scoring 'departing user' activity when the HR feed supplies a resignation or termination date. A contractor provided by an outsourcing firm downloaded 3,000 client documents in his last week, yet no departing-user alert fired, although his account was in the policy's scope. What is the most likely gap?

options.text: He came through procurement, so the HR feed held no end date for him and the trigger never started
The tool cannot monitor contractor accounts at all, so contractors must be covered by a separate product
3,000 documents is below the minimum volume that departing-user policies need before they raise any alert
He downloaded through the file-sync client, whose downloads are never recorded in the audit log

explanation.correct: A departing-user policy is only as good as its trigger. Microsoft Purview's 'Data theft by departing users' template, for example, starts scoring once resignation or termination dates arrive through the HR connector, or through the option to check for account deletion in Microsoft Entra. Contractors and outsourced staff are usually onboarded through procurement or a vendor-management system, not through HR, so their end dates never reach the HR feed. The fix is a process and data fix: add contractor engagement end dates to the HR data import, align account expiry with the contract end, and include contractors in the offboarding review. Banks rely heavily on outsourced staff, so this gap covers a large population.

distractors.b: The stem says his account was in scope; contractor accounts in the bank's directory are monitored like any other user, and the missing piece is the trigger.
distractors.c: There is no universal file-count minimum of this kind; the policy never started scoring because the trigger event never arrived.
distractors.d: Sync-client downloads are recorded in the Microsoft 365 audit log as FileSyncDownloadedFull; in any case a missing indicator would not explain why the departure trigger itself never started.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you look for gaps in the data that feeds a detection, not only in the detection logic.
